newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's defeated Gaullists seek new leadership.
newsitem.headline: France's defeated Gaullists seek new leadership.

text.p: France's Gaullist Rally for the Republic opened a special party congress on Sunday to choose a new leader it hopes will guide it out of the political wilderness following a disastrous election defeat.

The gathering of more than 4,000 RPR activists in the eastern Paris suburb of Vincennes was expected to anoint left-leaning nationalist Philippe Seguin, a potential rival to President Jacques Chirac, to head the party five weeks after it was swept from power in a June 1 parliamentary election upset.
Seguin would succeed arch-rival and former prime minister Alain Juppe, who orchestrated the campaign for the previous rightist majority.
Juppe stepped down as prime minister days before the June 1 runoff in the two-round election and, after initially hesitating, has now agreed to relinquish the Gaullist party reins.
There were five candidates for the top party job. Voting results were expected around 3.30 p.m. (1330 GMT).
"Our defeat was collective and the responsibility for it shared," said interim party leader and former interior minister Jean-Louis Debre in opening the party meeting.

The RPR congress is just one part of a recomposition of the defeated right, over which the weakened president, forced to yield much of his power to a left-wing government led by Socialist Lionel Jospin, has had only limited influence.
Seguin, the 54-year-old former National Assembly speaker, is a heavyweight orator who led the narrowly-defeated "no" campaign in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty on European union.
He has since said he generally favours the shift to the euro single currency and greater European integration.
Seguin has put his rhetorical talent to immediate use in attacking Prime Minister Jospin but has not yet come up with a coherent political line for the new opposition.

He has also pledged allegiance to Chirac, saying the role of a renovated RPR will be to "relay and support the president's initiatives". The two men have resumed weekly lunch meetings to discuss strategy.
Seguin's supporters and Juppe's have also buried the hatchet for the moment and will present a united front at Sunday's congress.

But Seguin has irked the head of state by cutting a deal with ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur's faction, and his associates have made clear they see him as a potential candidate to succeed Chirac when the president's term expires in 2002.

The president has spent much of the last two weeks trying to restore his influence in the party and help guide the rebuilding of the right, holding a series of individual meetings with party leaders and defeated members of parliament.

Tension between Chirac and Seguin has centred on the incoming leader's pledge to make Balladur's top lieutenant, former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, secretary-general of the RPR, the number two slot in the party.
Chirac's inner circle still regards Sarkozy as a traitor who betrayed the legitimate Gaullist leader to run Balladur's 1995 presidential campaign against him.

Balladur has insisted on the appointment of his associate as the price for his support of Seguin, but he acknowleged this week that the question may not be settled on Sunday but left until a national council meeting in the autumn.
